To defenestrate someone means to throw them out of a window. That's it — literal, physical, forceful. The window is the crucial detail. You cannot "defenestrate" someone through a door, off a rooftop, or out of any other opening. The word is window-specific.

You can defenestrate people or objects:

  • "The angry mob defenestrated the soldier." → They threw the soldier out of a window.
  • "She defenestrated her broken laptop." → She threw her laptop out of a window.

It works in passive form too: "He was defenestrated" simply means he was thrown out of a window (by someone).
The figurative meaning — and this is equally important

In modern usage, you'll actually encounter this word more often in a figurative sense, meaning: to abruptly and forcefully remove someone from a position of power or authority.

  • "The board defenestrated the CEO after the fraud was discovered." → The board suddenly and forcefully removed him from his role.
  • "The party defenestrated its own leader just before the election." → The party abruptly ousted its leader.

Notice what this figurative meaning captures that simpler words like "fired" or "removed" don't — it conveys the same quality as the literal act: sudden, forceful, and with no gentle landing. The person didn't resign gracefully; they were thrown out.

Defenestrate is not an everyday conversational word. It's rare, slightly formal, and carries a dramatic — sometimes even humorous — edge. When someone uses it, they're usually being deliberately vivid or clever. It signals: "I have a precise word for exactly this situation."

In writing and speech, it tends to land as either impressively specific, or wryly witty. Both are perfectly valid. The context tells you which.

FormExample
  • Present: "They defenestrate him" / "She defenestrates her opponents"
  • Past: "He defenestrated the minister"
  • Present participle: "They are defenestrating the old leadership one by one"
  • Noun form: defenestration — the act of throwing someone (or something) out of a window, or removing someone abruptly from power.

The most well-known use of this word in history is the Defenestration of Prague (1618), when a group of Protestant nobles threw Catholic royal officials out of a castle window during a political conflict. The officials survived (landing in a pile of rubbish below), but the event helped trigger a major European war. It's so famous that it made this word known to historians everywhere — and it's why you'll often see "defenestration" used almost playfully in political writing today, whenever someone powerful is abruptly ousted.
What makes this word worth knowing

Most languages don't have a dedicated single word for "throwing someone out of a window." English does. That specificity is what makes defenestrate genuinely useful — and memorable. It earns its place in the language by being precise in a way that no short substitute phrase quite matches.

When you want to say that someone was violently removed with zero ceremony — whether literally or from a position of power — this word does the job with vivid economy.
